summary: Defines the Application-Layer Traffic Optimization protocol, which lets ISPs share simplified network maps and cost information with applications so they can choose better endpoints. It is aimed at peer-to-peer and content delivery uses.

plainLanguage.summary: ALTO lets a network share a simplified view of endpoint locations and path preferences with applications. An application can use that information when it chooses which endpoint to contact.

subtitle: Lets a network publish simplified location and cost information for applications choosing endpoints.

tldr.problem: Applications that can choose among endpoints lack the network's view of locations and path preferences. Providers may also want to share useful guidance without exposing their full topology or actual costs.
tldr.mechanism: ALTO publishes network maps, costs between provider-defined groups, endpoint properties, and endpoint costs as JSON resources accessed over HTTP.
tldr.outcome: Applications can use the information when choosing endpoints, while providers control the abstraction and values they publish. RFC 7285 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9274.

today: RFC 7285 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2014. It has been updated by RFC 9274.

sections.title: What ALTO Shares
sections.content:
The Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) Protocol lets a network publish information about endpoint locations, path preferences, and endpoint properties. Applications that can choose among endpoints, such as peer-to-peer systems and content delivery networks, may use this information to change their choices.

An ALTO service represents a network's own abstract view. It does not expose the network's internal topology in this specification. A provider can abstract actual measurements into scores or rankings.
sections.plainLanguage: ALTO shares a simplified view of network locations and preferences. An application can use it to compare possible endpoints.

sections.title: Network Maps, PIDs, and Costs
sections.content:
A network map groups endpoint addresses into Provider-defined Identifiers (PIDs). A PID may represent a subnet, a point of presence, or another grouping chosen by the provider. A cost map gives costs for source and destination PID pairs, and the cost is directional.

The required routingcost metric uses lower values for higher preference. A cost mode says whether values are numerical or ordinal rankings. Clients can do arithmetic with numerical costs, but ordinal values are rankings and need not be unique or consecutive.

For IPv4 and IPv6 maps, longest-prefix matching maps an address to a PID. The map must cover every possible address and must not assign the same prefix to multiple PIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: A network map groups addresses into named PIDs. A cost map gives a directional preference between groups, and the cost mode explains how to read each value.

sections.title: The Four Information Services
sections.content:
The Map Service provides network maps and cost maps as batch information. The Map-Filtering Service lets a client ask for a subset of a map. A server may provide this filtering service.

The Endpoint Property Service looks up properties for individual endpoints, including the required pid property. The Endpoint Cost Service returns costs or rankings directly among endpoints. Each service is exposed through information resources announced by the server.
sections.plainLanguage: ALTO offers whole maps, filtered map results, endpoint properties, and endpoint costs. A server may provide these as separate information resources.

sections.title: Finding and Requesting Resources
sections.content:
ALTO uses HTTP requests and JSON-based media types for its resources. A client starts with a Root Information Resource Directory (IRD), which lists resource URIs, media types, and optional capabilities or dependencies. A Root IRD must identify a default network map; linked IRDs can list additional resources.

Clients use GET when a resource has no input parameters and POST when the request supplies parameters in a body. The methods are not interchangeable. Responses identify their media type, and an error response includes an ALTO error code as well as an appropriate HTTP status code.

Clients and servers must support HTTPS and TLS. Unknown JSON fields must be ignored so that extensions can add fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory tells a client which ALTO resources it can request. The client uses HTTP, and the response format identifies the kind of information returned.

sections.title: Using ALTO for Endpoint Choice
sections.content:
The RFC describes peer-to-peer examples. A tracker can fetch a network map and cost map, then provide a selected peer list to clients. A peer-to-peer client can also fetch the maps directly and use their costs in its own selection process.

Another example has a client collect candidate peers from other sources and ask the Endpoint Cost Service to rank them. The RFC notes that this example assumes the client and ALTO server are deployed by the same entity.
sections.plainLanguage: A peer-to-peer tracker or client can ask ALTO for location and cost information. It can use the answer when choosing among candidate peers.

sections.title: Security, Privacy, and Availability
sections.content:
False maps or cost information could direct many clients toward a small address range. ALTO uses HTTP over TLS to protect the authenticity and integrity of information between client and server, but authenticated guidance can still be undesirable or inaccurate. The RFC says an application may check results and disable ALTO or switch servers if its guidance is poor.

Maps can reveal network topology and policies, while endpoint queries can reveal client addresses or communication patterns. Providers should consider how much information to publish, and clients can use PIDs or less-specific prefixes when possible. Expensive queries can also burden a server, so access controls and pre-generated maps are discussed as protections.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS helps a client verify who supplied ALTO information, but it cannot guarantee the advice is good. Maps and queries can also reveal information about providers or users.
